In the interest of an informed electorate, look at how this works. In this particular case there are actually two ways it could work (meaning double profit for the US if they both happen, or a safety net if only one does).

Inflation Beats Interest

This is the classic and original method, that all large borrowers - banks and governments - have been doing for ages. Even (savvy) private citizens sometimes make this calculation for large loans (for real estate, usually).

Inflation is the process of the same dollar amount buying less (being "worth less") over time. This is why a gallon of gasoline used to cost 5 cents / gallon but is now 3-ish dollars. It's the same gas... but prices have inflated. When this happens to more or less all products at the same time and the same rate, that's inflation.

Imagine that you work one full 8-hour shift and get paid $100. You want to take a day off but can't afford to not be paid, so you borrow $100 and take the day off.

Imagine that loan was given to you at a 10% / year interest rate. If you pay that money back next year, you'll have to pay back $110.

Next year comes around, and prices have inflated. Now, you're paid $120 for your 8-hour shifts. You aren't richer, though, because everything else went up in price, too.

The time comes to pay back your loan. You don't have any cash to spare, so you pick up an extra 8-hour shift and are paid $120. You give $110 to your lender, and pocket $10. You got 8 hours off last year, and worked 8 extra this year, so you came out even, there. You borrowed $100 last year, and paid off the full loan + interest of $110 this year.

You made $10 "for free." What if instead of picking up that extra shift to pay off the loan, though, you borrowed the equivalent of an 8-hour shift - $120 - paid off the loan ($110), and kept that $10? Now you got 8 hours off last year and $10 in your pocket. You didn't have to work extra hours this year and you didn't have to take any cash out of your wallet this year.

Dafuq? By waiting a year, the value of the money you borrowed - the money you owed to your lender - decreased, because it was set at a fixed number while the rest of the world is free to adjust their numbers to the market. Your lender cannot go back and say "yo actually uhh I need 25% interest and you borrowed $110 not $100" after you the fact.

If you believe that prices will continue to inflate, then you make cash profit ($10) and real-world profit (an extra 8 hours of paid time off), by always borrowing to pay back your loans. The "Consumer Price Index" tries to track how prices have inflated over time in the US and really the Great Depression was the only time there wasn't inflation - so this is basically a sure thing. This is why our government does it. It's free money and free "real" value.

Foreign Exchange Rates

Since we're talking about China here, we can also play this game with foreign exchange rates. Unlike inflation, this is not a sure thing, and it is a bet.

But imagine: You borrow $100 USD from China at 10% interest. Actually, you borrow 100 RMB, which equals $100 USD, because the exchange rate is 1 dollar = 1 RMB.

A year later, the US economy is booming, Trump's tarriffs are hurting China, and Chinese companies all want to build in the US to avoid them so they need dollars. Now, it takes 2 RMB to buy just 1 dollar.

You decide to pay back your loan. You need to pay 110 RMB. You could take $55 out of your wallet and enjoy the $45 leftover from your original loan, which is now yours for free. But if you think the economic trend will continue, you could also borrow that 110 RMB from China, pay off your original loan, and now you get to keep all $110 USD in your wallet.

Which would you rather have? $45, or $110?
